newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil says won't bend to pressure on wages.
newsitem.headline: Brazil says won't bend to pressure on wages.

text.p: Brazil, Latin America's largest country, will not bend to demands from the United States, among others, for trade-linked labour standards at an upcoming global conference, Brazil's Foreign Minister said on Monday.

Luiz Felipe Lampreia, summing up Brazil's position ahead of next week's first ministerial encounter of the World Trade Organisation, said Brazil was in the clear majority in its opposition to the so-called "social clause".
The social clause links workers rights -- things like trade union affiliation, maternity leave and pension protection, for example -- to the opening of trade barriers.
"Brazil's position is shared by the vast majority and is opposed only by a few countries, principally the United States and France," said Lampreia.

"The Brazilian government is ... strongly opposed, like most countries, to the protectionist use of workers rights, or whatever discrimination against a country with lower wages or less developed living standards than others."

Brazil, like many developing nations, fears an attempt by countries like the United States at the WTO summit in Singapore to reduce its comparative wage advantage by tying a minimum set of workers rights to trade issues.

The issue of the "social clause" is one of a host of disagreements that threatens to turn the Dec. 9-13 meeting into a shouting match rather than the trouble-free encounter its organisers have been working feverishly to achieve.
"Singapore will not be just a formal meeting, but a meeting for negotiations," Lampreia conceded.
Brazil, among the world's 10 largest economies, will be going to the summit as one of the leaders of the southern hemisphere.

Lampreia underscored that Brazil condemns slave and child labour, both of which exist in Brazil. But he added that the government believed fundamental workers' rights came under the jurisdiction of the International Labour Organisation (ILO).
Lampreia also reiterated Brasilia's concern at pressure for faster liberalisation, not just within the framework of the WTO, but also with regard to the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
The creation of the FTAA, a hemispheric free trade zone due to come into being by 2005, has evolved into a low-key tussle between Washington and Brasilia.

Trade analysts say Brasilia is keen to ensure the Mercosur customs union, grouping Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay in addition to Brazil, is sufficiently consolidated to stand up to NAFTA -- the North America Free Trade Agreement -- before giant steps are taken towards the FTAA. NAFTA groups the United States, Canada and Mexico.
Nevertheless, Lampreia noted that every country had its own agenda based on domestic considerations. He also played down the significance of the discord.
"In international trade, there are no angels," he said.
